research_scope: Eleven findings on the 1943–1956 Ciudad Universitaria relocation, 1946 land decree, 1950–1954 construction and teaching, documented work crews, Central Library mosaics and 1952 stadium. Four broad-history, five POI-oriented, two specialist-technical. Two archival photo catalog records inspected; no reproduction rights granted.

findings.assertion: Before Ciudad Universitaria, university faculties were dispersed through adapted historic-centre buildings. UNAM's 2019 institutional historical account dates the selection of a Pedregal de San Ángel site to 1943, making relocation a history of urban decentralization, not simply a move to an already established university district.
findings.limitations: Selection and displacement described retrospectively; original planning correspondence, property ownership and affected local residents not researched

findings.assertion: UNAM's published history dates the presidential expropriation decree for the Pedregal lands to 11 September 1946, under Manuel Ávila Camacho. This records a claim about institutional land acquisition, not proof that there were no compensation or local land-tenure disputes.
findings.limitations: Original Diario Oficial decree, parcel boundaries, compensation and property titles not checked

findings.assertion: Three events must be distinguished: infrastructure work began in 1949, the campus foundation stone was laid 5 June 1950 according to UNAM IIE, and the official Dedicación was held 20 November 1952. First classes and major institutional relocation followed in March 1954, so 'opened in 1952' does not mean the complete teaching move occurred that year.
findings.source_locator: IIE introduction lines 2-5; UNAM Global 2019 lines 25-38,55-60; UNESCO description lines 2-5
findings.limitations: Different institutional definitions of inauguration and commencement; first-stone ceremony records and first-day teaching registers unexamined

findings.assertion: The university's 2019 retrospective gives 6,933 CU students in its first year, including 935 women, and says enrollment reached 25,000 in 1955. These institutional figures invite analysis of access to higher education, but they do not establish the socio-economic distribution of students or the entirety of women enrolled across UNAM.
findings.limitations: Original statistical yearbook and definition of first-year total not verified; 2019 source reports are historical numbers not current figures

findings.assertion: A UNAM photo catalog identifies Saúl Molina Barbosa's 1950–1952 photograph CKH000216 as workers performing foundation and column-assembly work at the central campus; this is specific surviving documentation of labor normally omitted by accounts limited to celebrated architects.
findings.source_locator: AFMT UNAM image CKH000216, catalog lines 7-22; visual preview of workers and site from catalog
findings.limitations: Exact photographed structure and worker identities unknown; preview is not a fully examined negative; rights clearance not established

findings.assertion: UNAM's architecture interview explains that the Estadio Olímpico was formed around a natural Pedregal depression, excavating and compacting local volcanic material into an embankment-like structure. This gives visitors a physical construction detail to inspect instead of repeating unsubstantiated claims of an original 'charro hat' or butterfly-shaped design.
findings.source_locator: Gaceta UNAM 17 Nov 2022 lines 16-26; expert María de Lourdes Cruz González Franco
findings.limitations: Original structural calculations and field fabric not checked; designer-inspiration interpretations explicitly disputed by cited specialist

findings.assertion: On the stadium's eastern side Diego Rivera created a stone-relief work, 'La Universidad, la familia y el deporte en México'. Gaceta UNAM reports that Rivera had intended to extend comparable work around the exterior, but the scheme was not completed; visitors should not mistake the extant mural for a finished full-perimeter decoration.
findings.limitations: Original artist design proposals and dates of interruptions absent; do not state definitive reason for non-completion

findings.assertion: The Central Library's four mosaic facades are intentionally differentiated: north references pre-Hispanic history; south conquest and colonial history; east twentieth-century social change; west the university and contemporary Mexico. The 1950s imagery records modern interpretations of earlier eras, not primary evidence of pre-Hispanic events.
findings.source_locator: Cultura/Conaculta O'Gorman 2012 article, historical facade summary; Eder 2011 journal abstract lines 46-49
findings.limitations: Full artist sketches and independent iconography monographs not yet collated; exact symbolic readings subject to interpretative debate

findings.assertion: The Library's first public opening should not be dated to the campus's 1952 dedication. The UNAM photo archive explicitly records that Biblioteca Central opened to its university community in April 1956, agreeing with Restrepo's 2019 abstract, while UNAM Global 2019 loosely lists the library among 1954 campus units; this definitional conflict remains to be reconciled.
findings.source_locator: AFMT CKH000064 lines 19-20, Restrepo 2019 abstract lines 27-32; UNAM Global 2019 lines 35-38
findings.limitations: Original April 1956 opening notice and 1954 inventory needed; do not equate shell building/administrative functions with public access

findings.assertion: A 2012 Secretaría de Cultura essay quoting O'Gorman's 1973 autobiographical account describes a test of three rows of colored-stone mosaic before Carlos Lazo approved the full library scheme, and reports work by approximately 60 people, including stoneworkers and mural setters. This is an attributed later reproduction of an artist's account, not an independently verified employment register.
findings.source_locator: Secretaría de Cultura 17 Jan 2012 lines 16-23, describing O'Gorman 1973 memoir
findings.limitations: Original 1973 autobiography not checked; quotation attribution and team count need confirmation with project payroll / memoir original

findings.assertion: Rita Eder's 2011 scholarly abstract interprets the Central Library's southern wall as presenting the competing Ptolemaic and Copernican cosmic models within a broader program about the collision and encounter of colonial cultures. This is a documented scholarly interpretation of a 1950s artwork, not a neutral illustration of colonial astronomy itself.
findings.source_locator: Eder 2011 Anales IIE DOI 10.22201/iie.18703062e.2011.98.2364, abstract lines 46-49
findings.limitations: Full Eder article not examined; visitor sightline and actual object-level panel matching not verified
